1.pericope_label: The plague examined: the signs, the priest, and the seven days

schools.summary: Gill explains that Aaron is named because the laws of leprosy fell to the priests, whose determination declared every plague clean or unclean. Calvin argues that appointing judges from the highest priestly order shows that spiritual service and not bodily health was in view, grants the contagion while denying that quarantine was the object, finds in the Hebrew idiom the dignity of a judgment proceeding from God, reads the seven days as a call to moderation, and turns the passage against the canonists who inferred a bishop's jurisdiction from the chief priest's and made confession necessary.

Henry insists the plague was an uncleanness rather than a disease, which is why priests and not physicians were employed and why Christ is said to cleanse lepers rather than cure them, draws from the delay that neither ministers nor people should be rash in censure or judge before the time, and notes that even the man pronounced clean washed his clothes, as an acquitted prisoner still goes down on his knees.

Clarke derives the Greek name from a word for a scale and the Hebrew from a verb to smite, with cognates meaning to cast down and to cause to cease, counts three marks of the disorder, and makes the idiom of pronouncing clean or unclean the proper measure of binding and loosing — an office of declaring the truth, not a power to cleanse or pollute. Wesley defines the priest's task as admitting to or excluding from the sanctuary, reads the whitened hair as a sign of corrupt humours and weak nature, and takes the washing of clothes to teach that no sin is too small to need washing.

Keil and Delitzsch render the three Hebrew terms as a lifting up, an eruption from a root meaning to pour out, and a bright spot from a root meaning to shine, and identify the two decisive marks as hair whitened on the spot and a spot sunken below the skin, noting that Arab practice still reckons the disease curable while the hair stays black. Ellicott supplies the colours the later authorities assigned to each symptom, the rule requiring two white hairs, and the grammatical usage by which a man is said to do what he officially declares done.

debates: Whether the separation of lepers was for contagion or for worship. Calvin allows the disease is catching but denies that public health was the point, since God gave the judgment to priests rather than to physicians.
What the verdict does. Clarke and Ellicott agree that the priest only declares what the signs already show; Calvin reads the same Hebrew form as investing the declaration with God's own authority.
outliers: Calvin's attack on the canonists, who reasoned from the chief priest's office to a bishop's jurisdiction and from spiritual leprosy to the necessity of confession, is far longer than his comment on the symptoms.
Clarke observes that the cognate roots of the Hebrew name mean to cast down and to cause to cease, because the disease obliges a man to cease from all work.
themes: the three signs of the plague

9.pericope_label: Old leprosy, the wholly whitened man, and the return of sound flesh

schools.summary: Gill reads the case as an inveterate and obstinate complaint beyond the reach of medicine, which is why the man goes to a priest rather than a physician, and applies it to the leprosy of sin as an old disease removable only by grace and the blood of Christ; he renders the general eruption as a flowering, the man appearing covered with white blossom.

Clarke asks why the partial leper is unclean and the wholly covered man clean, and answers from contagion: raw flesh yields an ichor that another's absorbent vessels take up, while a wholly dry scurfed surface offers nothing to imbibe, so only the partial disease is catching. He further speculates that a plague infecting bodies, clothes and house walls alike may have been caused by animalcula burrowing under the skin. Wesley explains the same paradox humorally, the partial eruption betraying an ill humour nature cannot expel and the total one proving nature has conquered and driven it outward, and observes that the warning about sound flesh is repeated because living flesh looks deceptively like health.

Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase for an old established leprosy, note that the priest pronounces at once without any shutting up since no doubt remains, gloss the Hebrew for raw flesh as properly meaning sustenance and so that which shows life, and call the complete whitening the crisis of the disease. Ellicott instead reads the case as the disorder re-appearing after cure, treats the two signs as alternatives, restricts the white-hair sign to hair still joined to the swelling that discoloured it, reports the lentil-sized minimum for a patch of sound flesh, and infers from the words in the day that there were days on which no inspection was made at all.

debates: Whether this second case is a recurrence or a long-standing disease. Ellicott takes it for leprosy returning after cure; Gill and Keil and Delitzsch read it as an old and inveterate complaint.
Whether the two signs are cumulative or alternative. Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley describe white rising, whitened hair and proud flesh together; Ellicott holds that either symptom alone suffices.

Why total covering makes a man clean. Clarke explains it by contagion, the dry surface being unable to transmit; Wesley by nature expelling the humour outward; Keil and Delitzsch by the eruption being the crisis of the disease.
outliers: Clarke's suggestion that the plague was caused by animalcula burrowing under the skin, offered to explain how it could infect garments and walls as well as bodies.
Ellicott's report that a patch of sound flesh had to be at least the size of a lentil to defile.
themes: the flowering of the whole skin
sound flesh as the worse sign

18.pericope_label: Leprosy rising out of a healed boil

schools.summary: Gill preserves the rabbinic definition of the boil as a hurt from wood, stone, pitch or hot water, and records a dissenting reading that refers the spreading to the ulcer rather than to the surrounding skin.

Henry surveys this case with the burn and the scall together, reading the re-opened sore as the danger of those who escape the pollutions of the world and are entangled again, the burn as the strife and contention that raises corruption to the surface, and the scall as a case where the verdict turned on the smallest of marks, black hair for soundness and yellow for the plague. He closes with two duties, to lament a life beset by troops of diseases that all entered by sin, and to give thanks for a sound constitution by glorifying God with the body.

Clarke reports a conjecture identifying the sore with the phlegmonic, erysipelatous, gangrenous and phagedenic ulcers of medical nomenclature, all brought before the priest to test whether they were infectious, and observes that a man already carrying a sore was likelier to take an infection than one whose skin was whole. Wesley notes that the word rendered dark may equally be rendered contracted.

Ellicott identifies the case as leprosy developing from an apparently healed boil, distinguishes that hurt from the burn by fire that follows, explains the white-reddish colour as peculiar to a re-opened scar and likens it to red wine poured into water, notes that the quarantine here is one week rather than two, and observes that the word leprosy has dropped from the Hebrew where the versions preserve it. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the alternative verdict as the closing or burning of the abscess, the skin killed by inflammation and falling away as scurf.

debates: What injury the boil denotes. Gill and Ellicott agree on the rabbinic list of wood, stone, pitch and hot water, expressly distinguished from actual fire; Clarke instead maps the term onto the ulcer classifications of modern medicine.
What the spreading proves. Ellicott takes it for evidence that the blood is already vitiated; Gill reports a reading that confines the spreading to the ulcer itself rather than the skin.
outliers: Henry converts the whole catalogue of sores into two devotional duties, lamenting the diseases that entered by sin and glorifying God for a sound body.
Ellicott's simile for the suspect colour, red wine poured into water, comes from the authorities who handled the disease rather than from the text.
themes: a verdict on the smallest mark

24.pericope_label: Leprosy rising out of a burn by fire

schools.summary: Gill defines the burning from his rabbinic sources as whatever is burnt by a coal or hot ashes, and so any sore raised by fire or by a thing heated in fire, and supplies the practical rule that on the seventh day the priest may look at any hour, without waiting for the day to end or the term to expire exactly — a rule he says holds everywhere in the chapter.

Wesley describes the burn as the touch of hot iron or burning coals, which naturally raises the ulcer in which the suspect spot appears, and glosses the closing verdict by referring it back to that same burning.

Ellicott distinguishes this burn by actual fire from the previous hurt by pitch or hot water, defends the margin's burning of fire against the text's hot burning, and renders the quick flesh as the sound new flesh that forms once the wound has drained; where the decisive marks appear he refers back to the symptoms already explained, and where they are absent to the directions already given for the boil. Keil and Delitzsch call the same thing the life of the scar, the skin forming over the burn and rising into a bright swollen spot, and state plainly that this case is to be treated exactly like the one before.

debates: How this case differs from the last. Ellicott and Gill both confine it to injury by actual fire, as against the pitch and hot water of the preceding case, and treat the distinction as deliberate.
outliers: Gill's rule that the priest need not wait out the seventh day exactly, which he extends to every similar expression in the chapter.
Keil and Delitzsch decline to distinguish the procedure at all, saying the case is handled exactly as the previous one.
themes: when the seventh day may be read

29.pericope_label: The scall on the head or the beard

schools.summary: Gill reads the wording to cover a man's beard or a woman's head and even a woman's beard, dates the second inspection to the thirteenth day from the first on rabbinic authority, and observes that the plague could still spread after a verdict of clean, so that the man remained subject to a fourth inspection. Calvin distinguishes leprous hair-loss from the baldness of age or of ordinary illness, neither of which pollutes, names the creeping and fox-like scurfs that resemble it, and reports the Oriental distinction between a forehead baldness the Arabian poets called noble, as coming of the helmet, and a hinder baldness they called servile.

Clarke reports the Jewish view that the disease made the hair drop out by the roots, and explains the unshaved scall on medical grounds, that shaving would inflame the place and give it appearances other than leprosy, leaving the priest unable to judge. Wesley marks the reversal of the sign, white hair in the body and yellow on the head, treats black hair as a sign of soundness and strength of nature, and says the shaving served the more certain discovery of the plague's growth or stay.

Ellicott notes that the distemper often attacks the hairy parts first, defines the dry scall from the canons as hair falling out by the roots, likens the golden hair to the new plumage of young pigeons, and reports the rules that only short yellow hair defiles and that two black hairs long enough to bow towards the root are needed for a verdict of clean; he also defends the Hebrew reading no black hair against the Greek's yellow, since on that emendation no ground for quarantine would remain. Keil and Delitzsch add the depression of the spot as the other symptom, and hold that once the eruption spreads after purification the priest need not look for yellow hair at all.

debates: Whether the text should read no black hair or no yellow hair. Ellicott defends the Hebrew against the Greek, arguing that the emendation would remove both unfavourable symptoms and leave no ground for quarantine at all.

Why the scall itself is left unshaved. Ellicott says it keeps the hair's colour visible, and describes leaving two hairs at each edge to show spreading; Clarke says shaving would inflame the place and confuse the diagnosis.
How far ordinary baldness resembles the plague. Calvin insists the baldness of age and of common illness do not pollute, and distinguishes the leprous loss from the creeping and fox-like scurfs.
outliers: Calvin's report that the Arabian poets ranked a forehead baldness noble, because it came of wearing a helmet, and a hinder baldness servile.
Ellicott's simile of young pigeons' new plumage for the golden hair, drawn from the authorities who handled the disease.
Gill's observation that a man pronounced clean stayed liable to a fourth inspection, since the scall might spread afterwards.
themes: the Hebrew defended against the Greek

38.pericope_label: The harmless white spots, and the provisos against mistaking deformity for plague

schools.summary: Gill notes that this provision covers man and woman alike.

Henry reads this case and the next as safeguards establishing that not every deformity is a ceremonial defilement, recalling that it was the children of Bethel, ignorant of God's judgments, who made a reproach of Elisha's baldness. He then marks the severity of the opposite verdict, the plague in the head being utter uncleanness answering to a corrupted judgment which few ever escape, and runs ahead to the convicted leper, whose condition he describes as the ruin of every earthly comfort though not itself a sin, whose rent clothes and covered lip he makes the pattern of penitent self-judging, and whose warning cry he distinguishes from contagion, since it was ceremonial defilement that the touch conveyed. The law, he concludes, could only teach the leper to cry unclean, whereas the gospel put into lepers' mouths a cry for mercy.
Wesley would render the word for the colour of the spots as contracted, or confined to the place where they are.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the harmless eruption by the name the Arabs still use, describing pale rings of unequal size that leave the hair untouched, cause no inconvenience, and last from two months to two years. Ellicott agrees that this complaint does not defile, places the spots chiefly on neck and face, and observes that the disorder still prevails in the East under the same biblical name, being a white scurf that runs a few months and disappears of itself.

debates: Whether the cry of the leper implies contagion. Henry denies it, holding that what the touch conveyed was ceremonial uncleanness rather than infection, so that the warning served the community's purity and not its health.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott can both still name this complaint from living usage, the Hebrew word for it surviving in Arabic to their own day.
Henry sets the law's compelled cry of unclean against the gospel cry of the ten lepers for mercy, making the one the disease and the other the help.
themes: the plague that does not defile

40.pericope_label: The bald head, and the sentence pronounced on the leper

schools.summary: Gill follows the rabbinic distinction between baldness running back to the neck and forward to the forehead, and notes that the law names only a leprous man because women did not commonly grow bald, an exception allowed only as something strange. Calvin reads the verdict's two halves as declaring the uncleanness and then charging the priest to sentence it, so that it should not enter the congregation, takes the plague upon his head for a just ignominy publicly inflicted, sets out the form of the sentence, observes that banishment outside the camp belonged to the desert years and was later replaced by expulsion from towns, doubts that the covered lip guarded against infectious breath and prefers to see in it the symbol of death worn by the civilly dead, and defends an active reading of the cry against a passive one on the strength of its emphatic repetition.
Wesley draws the inference the law is making, that such an eruption proves the baldness came not from age or accident but from the leprosy.

Ellicott concedes that baldness, though counted a disgrace and sometimes a divine punishment, is no sign of the plague, distinguishes baldness of the backhead from baldness of the forehead, likens the defiling eruption to the one arising in a healed boil, and reports how the later authorities supplied the procedure the text omits here, inferring from the words in appearance like the leprosy in the skin of the flesh that all the usual criteria apply, with sound flesh and spreading as the two operative marks since white hair cannot appear on a bald scalp. Keil and Delitzsch give the same two Hebrew terms the same senses and state that bald heads of both kinds were naturally clean.

debates: Why the covering of the lip was required. Calvin reports and doubts the view that it guarded others from infectious breath, preferring to read it as the mark of death worn by a man civilly dead.

Whether the leper cried out or was cried over. Calvin allows that the Hebrew form often bears a passive sense but prefers the active, since the doubled word is emphatic, while granting that a public proclamation may also have been made.

How a doubtful case of head-leprosy was handled. The text omits any remand; Ellicott records the later inference that the criteria given elsewhere were implied here, and the full two-week procedure built upon it.
outliers: Ellicott's observation that white hair is necessarily excluded from the criteria here, because the eruption appears on a scalp that has none.
Calvin's remark that the desert law of dwelling outside the camp was replaced, once Israel was settled, by expulsion from towns and villages.
themes: sentence lest it enter the congregation
the symbol of death on a living man

45.pericope_label: The leper's mourning dress, his cry, and his dwelling apart

schools.summary: Gill notes that the man was reckoned unclean and avoided as such for as long as the plague remained in him.

Henry weighs what the sentence cost — a stop to the man's business, severance from friends and relations, the ruin of every comfort — and makes his part a humbling under God's hand without insisting on his cleanness once the priest had spoken, which he turns into the penitent's confession of uncleanness in heart and life, by original corruption and by actual transgression. The exclusion he reads as a type of the purity to be kept in the gospel church.

Clarke has the leper mourn as for the dead, with the jaws bound in the manner used for corpses, a custom he says survived at Jewish funerals in Barbary, and takes the cry for a warning against contagion, noting that the Targum renders it as a caution to others rather than a confession. Wesley assigns a double purpose to each sign, sorrow and warning together, observes that the disease was not a sin though an effect of sin, and gives three reasons for the solitude: humiliation, the prevention of infection, and a lesson on the danger of company with spiritual lepers.

Ellicott grounds the mourning dress in the belief that leprosy was a visitation for the sufferer's own sin, renders the second sign as dishevelled hair rather than a bare head, explains the covered lip as veiling the beard, and reports that a herald sometimes went before the leper crying the warning. He then documents the reach of the seclusion, from the second-Temple rules on trees, synagogue compartments and marriage to their medieval Christian imitation, where the mass for the dead was read over the leper and he forfeited inheritance as a man legally dead. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the prescription and note that the separation lasted as long as the disease.

debates: Who uttered the warning. Clarke and Wesley take the cry as the leper's own; Ellicott records that a herald preceding him sometimes made it instead, following the Aramaic paraphrase.
Whether the covered lip was hygienic. Wesley allows that it served to preserve others from the man's breath or touch; Ellicott treats it purely as the veiling of the beard in mourning.
outliers: Ellicott's account of the medieval rite in which a priest read the service for the dead over a leper, threw earth on his feet, and left him barefoot in black, stripped of inheritance as a dead man.
Clarke's report that the binding of the leper's jaws matched the way the dead were bound, a funeral custom still observed among the Jews of Barbary.
Ellicott's detail that a leper standing under a tree defiled anyone who passed beneath it.

47.pericope_label: Leprosy in garments: what it was, and the first judgment

schools.summary: Gill lays out the question whether the plague in cloth was natural or miraculous, reports the Hebrew writers for the latter but inclines with Abarbinel to infection from the leper's own matter, which he says works between the threads and corrodes the texture; he prefers to read warp and woof as yarn still upon the spindle, records the dispute over whether the doubled colour-words weaken or strengthen the sense, and notes that the burning was done outside the city.

Henry calls the plague in a garment altogether unaccountable now and accepts that it was a sign and a miracle in Israel, an extraordinary punishment marking displeasure against a person or family, and notes that nothing was burnt on suspicion alone but had to be shown to the priest, since sentence must never rest upon a surmise.

Clarke attributes the fretting to small animals of the kind that cause the itch, breeding in the cloth and corroding it like moths, and supports the burning from reports that infected garments transmitted disease six or seven years later, as rag-sorters at paper mills had found. Wesley holds that diseases may be peculiar to particular ages and countries, argues that Moses would not have legislated about a fiction his people could refute, and dismisses the obscurity of warp and woof as immaterial now the law is abolished.

Ellicott argues from the identity of the phrase and of the symptoms that the same distemper is meant in cloth as in flesh, and refutes both the vermin theory and the contagion theory, marshalling the priest's close contact with lepers, the cleanness of the wholly covered man, the emptying of an infected house so its contents might be used again, and the canons exempting children, foreigners and bridegrooms; he tracks each step of the procedure against its human parallel. Keil and Delitzsch propose that the phenomenon was mildew, describing its appearance in linen and in leather, and resolve the warp-and-woof difficulty by referring the terms to prepared yarn.

debates: What the plague in garments actually was. Gill and Abarbinel make it infection from the leper's matter; Clarke makes it itch-mites fretting the cloth; Keil and Delitzsch make it mildew; Henry, Wesley and the Hebrew writers make it a miracle peculiar to Israel; and Ellicott refutes the first two by name.

Whether leprosy was contagious at all. Ellicott denies it outright and argues the point from the priest's own conduct and from the exemptions in the canons; Clarke and Gill both assume infection and reason from it.

What warp and woof denote. Gill reports Castalio's outer and inner side of the cloth but prefers unwoven yarn, as do Keil and Delitzsch in answering the objection that woven threads could not be infected separately.
Whether the doubled colour-words weaken or intensify. Gill gives one authority for greenish and reddish and another for exceeding green and exceeding red.
outliers: Clarke's report that garments carried the itch six or seven years after infection, and that rag-sorters at paper mills had found the same.
Ellicott's observation that dyed cloth and dyed skins could not contract the plague, which he counts as further proof that contagion was not in view.
Henry's note that a leprous spot needed to be no bigger than a bean to condemn the cloth.
themes: four theories of the plague in cloth

53.pericope_label: Washing, tearing out, and the second washing

schools.summary: Gill notes that the priest ordered the washing rather than performing it, that either the spot or the whole garment might be washed, and that the plague could reappear where nothing had shown before; he sees in the washing a figure of men's garments washed in the blood of Christ, and reads the closing formula as the rule by which priests were to judge cloth clean or unclean. Calvin declines the inquiry altogether, holding that God has mercifully willed this disease to be unknown, that the moth and the rust were given to keep the punishment of sin before our eyes, and that its expiation taught Israel to beware of external uncleanness — adding that insisting on the words would be superfluous labour, since it is not his purpose to perform the office of the grammarian.

Clarke explains the further seven days as time for the contagion to declare itself unequivocally, reports the rabbinic distinction between a first washing to remove the plague and a second to cleanse, and closes the chapter with a seven-point parallel between leprosy and sin, matching the hidden spot to original corruption, the diffusion to iniquity spreading through every appetite, the infectiousness to a sinner's precept and example, and the leper's confession to the humbling and the sacrifice by which guilt is taken away.

Ellicott rules that a spot keeping its suspicious colour must be burnt even without spreading, glosses the obscure verdict as a corroding in the fore or the hinder baldness of the cloth — the law describing a fabric's two faces as a forehead and the back of a head — has the darkened and contracted spot cut out and the garment cleared, and holds a reappearance to be incurable spreading leprosy; he also explains that the second washing was required even of stuff proved non-leprous. Keil and Delitzsch describe the tearing out of the paled spot and the washing that followed, and agree that a fresh outbreak was leprosy bursting forth again.

debates: Why a garment is burnt though the spot has not spread. Ellicott makes the retained colour itself decisive, the plague having eaten inward rather than widened.

What the two washings accomplish. Clarke reports the rabbinic division of the first as removing the plague and the second as cleansing; Ellicott holds the second was required even where the stuff proved never to have been leprous.
Whether the words repay close study. Calvin thinks insisting on them almost superfluous and declines the grammarian's office, while allowing the diligence of those who do examine them.
outliers: Ellicott's gloss by which the law names the two faces of a fabric its forehead and its hinder baldness.
Clarke's remark that only the universality of the evil keeps sinners from being expelled as monsters, since civil society is itself a leprous community.
Calvin's account of moth and rust as instruments by which God surrounds the race with rottenness so that the punishment of sin is always in view.
themes: leprosy as the emblem of sin
